topics.title: Chunk size and gleaning in LLM extraction
topics.what_it_is: You split the text before extraction. Large chunks need fewer LLM calls. But the model tends to extract fewer entities from a large chunk. Gleaning asks the model to look again at the same chunk and add what it missed.
topics.why: Chunk size sets the number of calls, the entity recall and the graph size. It is a cost and quality choice made before any retrieval.

io.inputs: Chunk size, gleaning rounds.
io.outputs: Number of entities extracted, number of calls.

formulas.verified: inferred: a simple counting estimate (ignores overlap and early stop of gleaning), not from the paper

steps: 1. Pick chunk size and overlap.
2. Extract.
3. Optionally glean up to g rounds.
4. Compare entity counts and cost across sizes on a sample.
topics.trade_offs: In the GraphRAG paper, on a HotPotQA sample GPT-4 extracted almost twice as many entity references with 600-token chunks as with 2400-token chunks. Gleaning let larger chunks keep quality (Appendix A.2, Fig. 3).

worked_example.spec: The pack's passages are 70 to 119 words (about 100 to 160 tokens), far below the 600 tokens above. It made 138 calls and 905 mentions (6.56 per passage). A chunk-size test on the pack would merge passages into 2x and 4x chunks and recount; to run later (small cost).
worked_example.computed_by: Read from the pack README and stats.json

topics.demo_hint: Slider: chunk size vs calls vs (paper-reported) entity count ratio.

topics.title: Coreference resolution
topics.what_it_is: Coreference finds all mentions that point to the same thing: 'Ridge regression', 'it', 'the method'. A model scores spans and links each mention to an earlier one. The result is a cluster of mentions per entity.
topics.why: If 'it' is not linked to 'ridge regression', the relation 'it was introduced by Hoerl' has no subject node. Per-passage LLM extraction in the pack handles pronouns only inside one passage.

io.inputs: A document.
io.outputs: Mention clusters.

symbols.epsilon: dummy antecedent (span starts no cluster), score fixed to 0
symbols.Y(i): candidate antecedents of span i plus the dummy

formulas.verified: paper-read: Lee et al. 2017, Sec. 3 (score s(i,j) and the softmax over antecedents)

steps: 1. Enumerate candidate spans.
2. Score mention-ness and pair links.
3. Pick an antecedent per span or the dummy.
4. Clusters = connected links.
5. Evaluate with MUC, B-cubed, CEAF (CoNLL-2012 average).
topics.trade_offs: Long documents are costly. Chunk-level extraction loses links across chunks. LLM pipelines often skip coreference and rely on name merging.

worked_example.spec: p002 has 'The theory', 'Ridge regression', 'its'. The LLM output names 'ridge regression' and 'ridge regression estimator (RR)' as two nodes. This is a real case of two mentions of related things kept apart. No coreference model was run.

topics.title: Distant supervision for relation extraction
topics.what_it_is: You have a knowledge base with known facts and a large unlabelled text. If a sentence contains both entities of a known fact, you treat it as an example of that relation. This gives you many labelled examples with no human labelling. The labels are noisy, because the sentence may not express the relation.
topics.why: It shows how to get training data for a relation extractor at scale. It also explains why edge quality needs a check even when the model looks good.

io.inputs: A knowledge base of triples and a text corpus.
io.outputs: Noisy labelled sentences and a trained relation classifier.

symbols.bag: all sentences that contain the pair (e1,e2)

formulas.verified: first part paper-read (Mintz 2009: the assumption that any sentence containing both entities of a KB relation expresses it); the max form (Riedel 2010, at-least-one) was not re-read: paywalled

steps: 1. Align entity pairs of the KB with sentences in the corpus.
2. Label each aligned sentence with the KB relation.
3. Relax: at least one sentence in the bag expresses the fact (Riedel).
4. Allow several relations per pair (Surdeanu).
5. Train a classifier; PCNN (Zeng 2015) selects the best sentence per bag.
topics.trade_offs: Cheap labels, but false positives from sentences that mention both entities without the relation, and false negatives from facts the KB lacks.

worked_example.spec: The pair (ridge regression, Hoerl) appears with introduced_by. A sentence such as 'Hoerl criticised ridge regression' would be labelled introduced_by by distant supervision and be wrong. Spec for later: build the bag of passages for this pair from the 138 and show the label noise.

topics.title: Entity linking to a knowledge base
topics.what_it_is: Entity linking maps a mention in text to one entry in a knowledge base, such as a Wikipedia page. It has two steps: find candidates, then pick the right one using the context. This is different from the query-to-graph-node linking in the retrieval page.
topics.why: A graph that links mentions to stable ids can join facts from many documents. Without ids, each document makes its own nodes.

io.inputs: A mention in context and a KB of entities with descriptions.
io.outputs: A KB id per mention, or NIL.

formulas.verified: paper-read: BLINK, Eq. 3 s(m,e)=y_m . y_e (dot product of two BERT encodings); the cross-encoder then re-ranks the retrieved candidates

steps: 1. Candidate generation (alias table, or dense retrieval).
2. Rank candidates with context (and coherence between mentions in AIDA).
3. Return NIL if no candidate fits.
4. Evaluate accuracy or micro-F1.
topics.trade_offs: Needs a KB with good descriptions. NIL detection is hard. GENRE generates names instead of ranking and needs a constrained decoder.

worked_example.spec: The pack links QUESTIONS to graph nodes (string match first, then embedding, cosine at least 0.55): 23 of 24 linked, 1 miss. That is the query side. Linking passage mentions to Wikipedia ids was not done.
worked_example.computed_by: Values read from entity_linking.json summary

topics.title: Entity resolution, step 1: blocking
topics.what_it_is: Entity resolution finds records that describe the same thing. Comparing all pairs is too slow. Blocking puts records into small groups (blocks) with a cheap key, and you compare only pairs inside a block. The loss is the true matches that land in different blocks.
topics.why: LLM extraction makes many near-duplicate node names. In the pack, 662 nodes give 218,791 pairs. Token blocking cuts this to 3,551 pairs.

io.inputs: Records (node names, with type).
io.outputs: A set of candidate pairs.

symbols.E: all pairs a brute-force run would compare (n(n-1)/2 for deduplication of n records)

formulas.verified: paper-read: Papadakis et al. 2020 survey, blocking measures PC, PQ, RR (they cite earlier sources; the earliest definition was not traced)

steps: 1. Choose a block key (a shared token, a sorted-neighbourhood window, a hash).
2. Build an inverted index from key to records.
3. Form pairs inside each block.
4. Report RR and PC (PC needs gold matches).
topics.trade_offs: A coarse key keeps recall and gives many pairs. A fine key gives few pairs and loses matches. Schema-agnostic token blocking suits messy names.

worked_example.spec: Token blocking on lower-case words with a plural s removed and the words {of, the, and, a, in, for, to, on, with, data, model, models} ignored. A pair enters C if the two names share at least one remaining word.
worked_example.computed_by: Recomputed in build.py. PC cannot be computed: the pack has no gold duplicate pairs. The stop-word list is our choice and changes the counts.

topics.demo_hint: Slider: the stop-word list and the block size cap; watch pairs and RR change.

topics.title: Entity resolution, step 3: clustering and how to score it
topics.what_it_is: Pair decisions must become clusters, because 'a=b' and 'b=c' implies 'a=c'. You take the transitive closure or use a clustering step. You then score the clusters against gold clusters with B-cubed or pairwise precision and recall.
topics.why: Merging by chains can pull in a wrong third node. You need a score to tune the thresholds, and the pack has no such score yet.

io.inputs: Match decisions or probabilities; gold clusters for scoring.
io.outputs: Entity clusters (one cluster = one graph node) and scores.

symbols.w_d: weight of mention d (equal weights in the paper)

formulas.verified: paper-read: Bagga and Baldwin 1998 (COLING-ACL), Sec. 7.3: per-entity precision and recall, final scores as weighted sums, equal weights 1/N

steps: 1. Build a graph of accepted matches.
2. Take connected components, or cluster by a correlation score, to avoid long chains.
3. Pick a canonical name and keep aliases.
4. Score with B-cubed against a labelled sample.
5. Send the biggest clusters to a human look.
topics.trade_offs: Transitive closure is simple and can over-merge. Pairwise and B-cubed scores answer different questions.

worked_example.spec: Build the 50-pair gold sample by a human from the top candidate pairs, then compute B-cubed for the pack's merge rule and for a Jaccard>=0.75 rule. Not done: no gold exists.
worked_example.computed_by: B-cubed and pairwise P/R/F1 computed in the entity_resolution demo (data demos/data/er_bcubed.real.json) on a seeded sample of 60 nodes with our gold clusters: pack as built B-cubed P 0.985 / R 0.910 / F1 0.946, pairwise P 0.857 / R 0.429 / F1 0.571; definition read in Bagga and Baldwin 1998 Sec. 7.3, F1 as harmonic mean is our addition.

topics.demo_hint: Pairs to clusters: draw the chain a=b=c and the over-merge.

topics.title: Entity resolution, step 2: matching
topics.what_it_is: For each candidate pair, decide match or no match. Classic methods compare fields with string similarity and add weights (Fellegi-Sunter). Neural methods read both records (DeepMatcher, Ditto). Recent work asks an LLM directly.
topics.why: Matching decides which duplicate nodes merge. A false merge joins two different things and creates wrong paths. A missed merge splits the evidence. Both change GraphRAG answers. In our graph: an LLM judge (Claude Opus 5.5) decided 8,329 candidate pairs, and 7,538 name groups became 6,814 concepts. In a side test without the LLM, the best matcher (bge-m3 cosine ≥ 0.90) reached F1 0.41 against the LLM decisions, and fuzzy token-set matching chained names into one 801-name cluster; so string and vector similarity only propose candidates (blocking), and the decision reads the passages.

io.inputs: Candidate pairs with names, types, descriptions.
io.outputs: Match probability or label per pair.

symbols.u_i: P(field i agrees | records do not match)
symbols.w: total weight; above an upper threshold = match, below a lower one = non-match, between = clerical review

formulas.verified: standard-not-reread: Fellegi-Sunter weights as commonly written; Jaccard is the standard definition

steps: 1. Compute similarity features per pair (token Jaccard, edit distance, embedding cosine, same type).
2. Score with weights, a classifier, or an LLM prompt.
3. Choose thresholds on a labelled sample.
4. Send the grey zone to review.
topics.trade_offs: Rules are cheap and explainable. Neural models need labelled pairs. LLMs need no labels but cost tokens and vary. The pack's own rule (below) uses no similarity at all and so keeps near-duplicates by design.

worked_example.spec: Real candidate pairs from the blocking step, scored by token Jaccard. The pack's merge rule merged only 4 abbreviation pairs (LASSO, OLS, PCR, PLS). Pairs such as 'linear regression' and 'linear regression models' stay as two nodes.

abbreviation_merges: least absolute shrinkage and selection operator

worked_example.computed_by: Recomputed in build.py; these are CANDIDATES, not verified matches (no gold).

io.outputs: Triples scored against gold.

3. Match against gold.

topics.title: What extraction costs
topics.what_it_is: LLM extraction costs one call per chunk, plus gleaning rounds, plus summaries (and community reports in GraphRAG). The cost equals tokens times price. Indexing is paid once; query cost differs by method.
topics.why: Index cost decides if a method fits a corpus. The LightRAG paper compares retrieval-time tokens: GraphRAG used about 610 community reports of about 1,000 tokens each (610,000 tokens) on its Legal dataset, and LightRAG used fewer than 100 tokens (paper's own count).

io.inputs: Tokens in and out per call, number of calls, price.
io.outputs: USD per corpus and per update.

steps: 1. Estimate calls from corpus size and chunk size.
2. Measure tokens on a 5% sample.
3. Multiply by the price.
4. Add summaries and reports.
5. Add update cost: LightRAG re-runs only new chunks; GraphRAG may regenerate community reports (paper: about 5,000 tokens per report, 1,399 communities).
topics.trade_offs: A cheap model (as in the pack) makes indexing cheap but may lower extraction quality. The cost claims above are from the LightRAG authors, who compare against GraphRAG, so treat them as one side's numbers.

worked_example.spec: Real cost of the pack: 138 calls, 47,819 prompt tokens, 57,252 completion tokens, USD 0.02727.
worked_example.computed_by: Division in build.py. Extrapolation assumes the same passage length and price; not a quote.

topics.title: Microsoft GraphRAG: the indexing pipeline
topics.what_it_is: GraphRAG splits the corpus into chunks. An LLM extracts entities (name, type, description) and relations (source, target, description) from each chunk. The same entity from different chunks is merged, and descriptions are summarised. The graph is then split into communities with the Leiden algorithm, and the LLM writes a report per community.
topics.why: The community reports make global questions possible ('what are the main themes?'). The cost is paid once at indexing time, in many LLM calls.

io.inputs: Text chunks, extraction prompt, chunk size, number of gleaning rounds.
io.outputs: Entity graph, community partition, community reports.

steps: 1. Chunk the text (default window 600 tokens in the paper's setup).
2. Extract entities and relations per chunk with an LLM.
3. 'Glean': ask the model if entities were missed and extract more, up to a maximum number of rounds.
4. Merge equal entities, summarise their descriptions.
5. Leiden community detection (hierarchical).
6. Write a report for each community.
topics.trade_offs: More chunk calls and gleaning cost tokens; larger chunks are cheaper but lose entities. See the chunk-size topic.

worked_example.spec: The pack follows this recipe in a reduced form: per-passage extraction (no gleaning), rule-based alias merge, Leiden (57 communities), 15 LLM community reports.

topics.title: HippoRAG: OpenIE graph with synonymy edges
topics.what_it_is: HippoRAG asks an LLM for named entities first, then for triples that include them, so the graph holds noun phrases and not only named entities. It adds a synonymy edge between two phrase nodes when the cosine similarity of their embeddings is above a threshold tau. It also keeps a matrix of how often each phrase appears in each passage.
topics.why: The synonymy edges link near-duplicate names without merging them. Personalized PageRank then spreads over these links at query time.

io.inputs: Passages P, an LLM, a retrieval encoder M.
io.outputs: A schemaless KG, synonymy edges E', and a phrase-by-passage count matrix.

symbols.tau: synonymy threshold (0.8 in the paper's setup)
symbols.P: counts of each phrase in each passage

formulas.verified: paper-read: Sec. 3 'Offline Indexing' and the hyper-parameter note in Sec. 4 of the HippoRAG paper

steps: 1. Extract named entities from each passage.
2. Extract triples with those entities in the prompt (OpenIE).
3. Add synonymy edges with cosine at least tau.
4. Build the phrase-by-passage matrix.
5. At query time: link query entities, run PPR, rank passages (see J3 and the PPR entry).
topics.trade_offs: Schemaless means no schema design but also no type control. Synonymy edges depend on the encoder. HippoRAG 2 adds passage nodes and better query linking.

worked_example.spec: Use the pack's near-duplicate pairs from the blocking topic as the pairs that a synonymy edge would link (for example ridge regression and ridge regression estimator). Cosine values need the MiniLM vectors of node names: to compute later.

topics.title: Joint entity and relation extraction
topics.what_it_is: A pipeline finds entities first and relations second, so an entity error spreads to the relations. A joint model learns both tasks together. Methods tag the text with a combined scheme (Zheng et al.), score spans and pairs (SpERT), or generate triples as text (REBEL, UIE).
topics.why: Joint models cut error propagation and run in one pass. Generative models such as REBEL output triples directly, which is the same idea as the LLM prompt.

io.inputs: Raw sentences.
io.outputs: Entities and relations from one model.

formulas.verified: standard-not-reread: typical joint objective; each paper uses its own variant

steps: 1. Encode text with a shared encoder.
2. Score entity spans.
3. Score relations between candidate spans (or generate linearised triples).
4. Train on both losses together.
topics.trade_offs: Less error propagation and faster. Needs labelled joint data (or a generative model). Overlapping triples need careful design.

worked_example.spec: The LLM prompt is joint: one call returns entities and relations. A check: all relation endpoints must be in the entity list (rule in the prompt). Count violations later.

topics.title: From raw data to a knowledge graph: the whole pipeline
topics.what_it_is: A knowledge graph (KG) is built from data in stages. First you get the data (text, tables, PDFs, databases, APIs). Then you find the things (entities) and the links between them (relations). Then you merge duplicates and write the result into a graph store. Each stage can fail, and each failure changes what the graph can answer later.
topics.why: GraphRAG and LightRAG answer questions only from the graph they get. If an entity is missing or split in two, the retriever cannot find it. The data problem comes before the retrieval problem.

io.inputs: Raw sources: free text, parsed PDFs, tables, relational databases, API records.
io.outputs: A graph: nodes (entities with type and description), edges (typed relations with the source passage), and a pointer from each node and edge back to the text it came from.

steps: 1. Acquire and parse the source (see J2 for parsing and chunking).
2. Split into units the model can read (passages or chunks).
3. Entity recognition (NER) and relation extraction (RE), by rules, a trained model, or an LLM prompt.
4. Coreference inside a document and entity linking or entity resolution across documents.
5. Choose a schema (closed list of types) or keep it open, then canonicalise names and relation labels.
6. Write to a store: property graph or RDF.
7. Check quality: parse failures, isolated nodes, duplicates, a human sample.
topics.trade_offs: Surveys group the work into LLM-augmented KG construction (Pan et al.), generative construction (Ye et al.) and knowledge acquisition (Ji et al.). Fixed pipelines are cheap and predictable. LLM pipelines need no training data but cost tokens and can hallucinate relations.

topics.title: Quality control of an LLM-built graph
topics.what_it_is: Quality means the graph is correct, complete and consistent. Surveys list dimensions and metrics (accuracy, completeness, consistency) and describe refinement (finding wrong or missing facts). For an LLM-built graph, you check parse failures, schema conformance, isolated nodes, duplicates, and a human sample of triples.
topics.why: Nobody checks a graph that feeds a retriever, so errors silently lower answer quality.

io.inputs: The graph and its source passages.
io.outputs: A quality report and a list of fixes.

formulas.latex: \text{triple precision}=\frac{\#\ \text{triples judged correct in a random sample}}{\#\ \text{triples sampled}}

symbols.sample: random sample of triples with their source passage shown to a judge

formulas.verified: inferred: standard sampling estimate; report a confidence interval

steps: 1. Count parse failures and schema violations.
2. Look at structure: isolated nodes, component sizes, degree, nodes seen in one passage only.
3. Sample triples with their passage and judge them.
4. Estimate duplicates by blocking and a human sample.
5. Fix prompts and rules; rebuild; compare.
topics.trade_offs: Structure checks are cheap and weak. Human sampling is strong and slow. An LLM judge is cheaper but needs its own validation.

topics.title: LightRAG: the indexing pipeline
topics.what_it_is: LightRAG builds the graph in three functions: Recog extracts entities and relations from each chunk, Prof makes a key-value pair for each node and edge (index keys plus a text summary), and Dedupe merges equal entities and relations. When new documents come, it runs the same steps on them and takes the union with the old graph.
topics.why: The key-value profiles are what the dual-level retrieval searches. The union update avoids a rebuild.

io.inputs: Chunks of documents D.
io.outputs: A graph with key-value profiles for every node and edge.

symbols.Recog: LLM extraction of entities and relations

formulas.verified: paper-read: Eq. 2, Sec. 3.1 of the LightRAG paper (arXiv text lines 174-190)

steps: 1. Split the documents into chunks.
2. Recog: extract entities and relations.
3. Prof: keys and summary text for each node and edge (entities use the name as key; relations may have several keys).
4. Dedupe: merge identical entities and relations across chunks.
5. Update: process only new documents with the same steps and take the union.
topics.trade_offs: The paper reports that retrieval needs far fewer tokens than GraphRAG community reports. See the cost topic. Dedupe is exact-match style, so near-duplicates need more.

topics.title: LLM prompt-based extraction
topics.what_it_is: You give an LLM a passage and an instruction, and it returns entities and relations as JSON. You can add a schema, a few examples and a rule such as 'use only what the passage says'. No training is needed. The cost is one call per chunk.
topics.why: This is how GraphRAG, LightRAG and HippoRAG build their graphs. It is also the method behind the real graph in the pack: 138 calls, temperature 0.

io.inputs: Passage, type list, relation list, output format, optional examples.
io.outputs: JSON with entities and relations; the code parses it and counts failures.

formulas.verified: inferred: accounting identity, not from a paper

steps: 1. Write the prompt: task, closed lists, 'only what the passage states', output format.
2. Call the model with temperature 0 and ask for JSON.
3. Parse; count failures (the pack had 0 of 138).
4. Map unknown labels to a fallback (the pack maps them to related_to or Other).
5. Cache every response so a rerun is free and identical.
topics.trade_offs: Flexible and good at coverage. topics.title: Named entity recognition (NER)
topics.what_it_is: NER finds spans of text that name things and gives each span a type, such as person, place, organisation or method. It is the first step of most extraction pipelines. Early systems used rules and gazetteers. Next came feature-based taggers. Today a transformer encoder tags each token, or an LLM lists the entities in a prompt.
topics.why: Every node in the graph starts as an entity mention. A missed mention is a missing node. A wrong type puts the node in the wrong group.

io.inputs: A passage of text and a list of entity types.
io.outputs: Spans with start, end, type (and often a confidence).

symbols.TP: predicted spans with exact boundaries and the right type
symbols.FP: predicted spans not in the gold set

formulas.verified: standard-not-reread: CoNLL-2003 scores exact-match entity-level F1

steps: 1. Define the type list (a closed list, or open).
2. Tag tokens with BIO labels (B begin, I inside, O outside) or output a span list.
3. Decode spans from the tags (a CRF layer enforces valid tag order).
4. Score with entity-level F1 against gold spans.
5. For an LLM prompt, parse the JSON output and count failures.
topics.trade_offs: Trained taggers are fast and cheap but need labelled data per domain. LLM prompts work zero-shot on new types but vary run to run and cost tokens. Exact-match scoring punishes a boundary that is off by one word.

topics.title: Open information extraction (Open IE)
topics.what_it_is: Open IE extracts triples whose relation is a phrase from the text, so you do not need a relation list. A system reads a sentence and returns (subject phrase, relation phrase, object phrase). HippoRAG uses an LLM for this step and builds its graph from the phrases.
topics.why: Open labels keep facts that no schema foresaw. They also create many surface forms of the same thing, so a graph from Open IE needs merging later.

io.inputs: Sentences or passages.
io.outputs: Phrase triples (arg1, relation phrase, arg2).

steps: 1. Parse or prompt to find a relation phrase and its arguments.
2. Filter incoherent or vague relations (ReVerb constraints).
3. Add context conditions if needed (OLLIE).
4. Canonicalise phrases to nodes (see canonicalisation topic).
topics.trade_offs: High coverage, noisy and unnormalised. TextRunner was a one-pass system. ReVerb improved precision with syntactic and lexical constraints. Stanovsky et al. made it a supervised tagging task.

topics.title: Pattern-based extraction (Hearst patterns)
topics.what_it_is: You write lexical and syntactic patterns that signal a relation, such as 'X such as Y' for is-a. A pattern matches text and outputs a triple. The method needs no training data. It is exact when it matches and it misses most facts.
topics.why: Patterns are the cheap, auditable baseline. Teams use them for high-precision seeds, for definitions in glossaries, and as a check on LLM output.

io.inputs: Text and a list of patterns.
io.outputs: Triples with the matched pattern as evidence.

steps: 1. Write a pattern (for example 'NP such as NP, NP and NP').
2. Match it on tagged text.
3. Emit (hypernym, is_a, hyponym) for each match.
4. Measure precision on a sample, then add or drop patterns.
topics.trade_offs: High precision, low recall, language and domain specific. Each new relation needs new patterns.

topics.title: Property graph versus RDF: where to store the graph
topics.what_it_is: Two main models hold a KG. RDF stores facts as triples (subject, predicate, object) with global identifiers. A property graph has nodes and edges that carry labels and key-value properties. RDF* adds statements about statements and brings the two models closer.
topics.why: GraphRAG tools use property graphs (Neo4j, networkx). Semantic-web tools use RDF. The model decides how you attach the source passage, a confidence or a date to an edge.

io.inputs: Triples with provenance.
io.outputs: A stored graph and its query language (Cypher and similar, or SPARQL).

steps: 1. List what you must attach to an edge (source passage, score, time).
2. If edges need properties, choose a property graph or RDF*.
3. If you must share a vocabulary or reason with OWL, choose RDF.
4. Keep a mapping between the two.
topics.trade_offs: Property graphs are easy for engineers and for traversal. RDF has standards and reasoning. Plain RDF needs reification to annotate a triple, which is clumsy.

topics.title: Reading a built graph: what the numbers tell you
topics.what_it_is: A few numbers describe a graph: node and edge counts, mean degree, degree distribution, connected components. They show if the graph is connected enough for multi-hop retrieval. They do not show if the facts are true.
topics.why: If the largest component holds only part of the nodes, a walk from a query seed cannot reach the rest.

io.inputs: Nodes and edges.
io.outputs: Summary statistics.

steps: 1. Make the undirected simple graph.
2. Count nodes, edges, components.
3. Compute mean and max degree.
4. Plot the degree distribution.
5. Look at the top-degree nodes.
topics.trade_offs: Generic hub nodes (regularization, 27 links) help recall and add noise to seeds. Many degree-1 nodes mean most entities appear once.

topics.title: Relation extraction (RE): the task and its families
topics.what_it_is: Relation extraction decides which pairs of entities in a text are linked and by which relation. The families are: patterns, supervised classifiers, distant supervision, Open IE, joint models and LLM prompts. They differ in where the relation list and the training signal come from.
topics.why: Edges carry the multi-hop paths that GraphRAG walks. A wrong or vague edge sends the walk to the wrong place. The pack's graph shows this: 117 of 762 edges (15%) use the vague label related_to.

io.inputs: A passage with entity mentions (or the raw passage) and a relation list (or none).
io.outputs: Triples (subject, relation, object), each tied to a passage.

formulas.verified: standard-not-reread: the classification form of supervised RE

steps: 1. Choose the relation list (closed) or allow free text (open).
2. Choose the signal: hand rules, labelled data, a knowledge base, or an LLM prompt.
3. Predict a relation per entity pair, or generate triples directly.
4. Keep the source passage with each triple.
5. Score with P/R/F1 against gold triples when you have them.
topics.trade_offs: Closed lists give clean graphs and miss new relations. Open labels catch everything and need canonicalisation later. The no-relation class dominates the pairs, so precision is the hard part.

topics.title: Schema-guided versus open extraction, and canonicalisation
topics.what_it_is: Schema-guided extraction gives the model a closed list of types and relations (or an ontology). Open extraction lets it write any label. Open output needs a canonicalisation step that maps labels to a schema. EDC does this in three phases: extract openly, define each label in words, then canonicalise by matching definitions.
topics.why: Closed lists give a clean graph that queries can use. Open labels give coverage. The choice sets how much merging work comes after.

io.inputs: Text; optional ontology or type and relation lists.
io.outputs: Triples whose labels belong to the schema.

steps: 1. Decide closed, open, or open-then-canonicalise.
2. If closed: put the lists in the prompt and map unknown labels to a fallback.
3. If open: extract, define each label, embed the definitions, map to the nearest schema label above a threshold.
4. Measure conformance: share of triples whose relation and types are in the schema.
topics.trade_offs: Closed lists force facts into the wrong label or into related_to. Open labels explode the vocabulary. Ontology-driven benchmarks (Text2KGBench) show that conformance and hallucination need separate metrics.

worked_example.spec: The pack is schema-guided: 9 entity types and 13 relation labels in the prompt. Counts: related_to (117 edges) is the second most common label after uses (149); it is the model's vague fallback.

topics.title: Tables, databases and APIs as graph sources
topics.what_it_is: Structured data already has entities and links: a row is an entity, a column is a property, a foreign key is a relation. You map it to a graph with rules instead of reading text. The W3C direct mapping gives one default rule set. R2RML lets you write your own mapping.
topics.why: Many RAG projects hold facts in SQL tables or API records. A rule mapping is exact, cheap and repeatable. An LLM is not needed for the keys and the foreign links. You need it only for free-text columns.

io.inputs: Relational schema and rows, or JSON records from an API, or a CSV table.
io.outputs: RDF triples or property-graph nodes and edges, one per row and per foreign key.

formulas.latex: \text{row } r \in T \;\Rightarrow\; \text{node } \langle T,\,\mathrm{pk}(r)\rangle;\qquad \text{cell } r[c] \;\Rightarrow\; \text{property } (T{\#}c,\; r[c]);\qquad \text{FK } r[c]\!\to\! r' \;\Rightarrow\; \text{edge } (r,\; T{\#}c,\; r')
formulas.verified: standard-not-reread: this is the direct-mapping idea of the W3C Recommendation; exact IRI rules are in the spec

steps: 1. List tables, primary keys and foreign keys.
2. Apply the direct mapping, or write an R2RML mapping.
3. For free-text columns, run the text pipeline (NER, RE) on the cell.
4. Keep the source row id on every node, so you can trace and refresh.
5. For an API, fetch records on a schedule and map each field by a small config.
topics.trade_offs: Rule mapping is exact but only as good as the schema. Join tables and codes need a manual mapping. Tables in PDFs are a parsing problem first (J2). Text-to-SQL at query time (J3) is another way to use such data without building a graph.
